547.title: Deeds without measure (Mishnah Peah 1:1)
547.hook: the morning service lists things with no limit: honoring parents, kindness, hospitality, visiting the sick
547.howItsDone: Many prayer books place the Mishnah Peah passage and the list from tractate Shabbat right after the blessings over Torah study, so that each morning begins with a little learning about kindness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, neshamah, the soul the morning prayer calls pure. Your line was the soul is pure. Did you answer the critic? Today, a list read every morning, of things that have no ceiling. Day five hundred forty-seven.

Almost everything in a life of practice has a size. So many minutes of prayer. So many words in a blessing. A tenth of the harvest. Rules like that are a gift: you know when you've done it. But early in the morning service, many prayer books include a passage that goes the other way. It names a handful of things and says: these have no measure. Nobody can tell you that you've done enough of them. It's a short list, and it starts in a farmer's field.
screen: `EVERYTHING HAS A SIZE.` → `YOU KNOW WHEN YOU'RE DONE.` → `THESE HAVE NO MEASURE.`

segments.voice: The passage is the opening of the Mishnah, tractate Peah. It says: these are things that have no measure. Peah, the corner of the field. The Torah tells farmers not to harvest the edges of their fields but to leave them for the poor and the stranger, and it never says how big the corner should be. Then the first fruits, and the pilgrim's offering at the Temple. Then gemilut chasadim, acts of loving-kindness. Then the study of Torah. None of them has a set size. The rabbis later set a minimum for the corner, one sixtieth of the field, and no maximum. Then the prayer book adds a second list, from the Talmud, tractate Shabbat: things whose fruit you enjoy in this life, while the principal stays for the world to come. Honoring your father and mother. Acts of kindness. Taking in guests. Visiting the sick. Helping a bride marry. Walking with the dead to their burial. Making peace between people. And it ends: the study of Torah is equal to them all, because study is meant to lead to doing. Why put this list in the morning, right after the blessings for waking? One reading: you've just thanked God for your eyes and legs and strength. Now here's what they're for. The Jerusalem Talmud adds a careful note: giving money has limits, so you don't impoverish yourself, but kindness done with your own body, your time, your presence, has none.
screen: `MISHNAH PEAH: NO MEASURE.` · `THE CORNER OF THE FIELD.` · `FRUIT NOW, PRINCIPAL LATER.` · `MONEY HAS LIMITS; PRESENCE DOESN'T.` · then, large: `NO LIMIT ON KINDNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose one of them for today. Settle, and breathe. Let the list pass slowly in front of you. Honoring a parent. A guest. Someone sick. Someone grieving. Two people who aren't speaking. Notice which one makes you think of a real name. Stay with that person. Picture the smallest version of the deed: a phone call, a visit, a meal, a sentence that might make peace. Picture yourself doing it, today, and what time it would be. The bell holds the time.
Deeds without measure. From the Mishnah: kindness, the corner of the field and study have no set size, said each morning.
Your line: no limit on kindness. Today, do the deed you pictured, and when you've done it, notice the pull to do one more. Day five hundred forty-seven.

548.title: Learning before breakfast
548.hook: the day begins with a blessing over Torah, then a little study straight away
548.howItsDone: Jews who pray each morning say the blessings over the Torah early in the service, then immediately read a few short passages, often the priestly blessing, a mishnah and a passage of Talmud, so the blessing covers the day's study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, deeds without measure, the list of things with no ceiling. Your line was no limit on kindness. Did you do the deed you pictured? Today, the blessing that comes just before that list. Day five hundred forty-eight.

Most of us start the day by taking something in. Headlines. Messages. Somebody else's photos of somebody else's breakfast. Whatever comes first tends to set the weather for the rest of the morning. The Jewish prayer book has an opinion about what should come first. Very early, before the psalms, before the main prayers, before a single request, there's a blessing for studying Torah. And then, so the blessing isn't left hanging in the air, a few lines to actually study, right there, on the spot.
screen: `WHATEVER COMES FIRST SETS THE WEATHER.` → `A BLESSING FOR STUDY.` → `THEN STUDY, ON THE SPOT.`

segments.voice: The blessing comes from the Talmud, tractate Berakhot, where several rabbis each offer their own wording, and the prayer book keeps more than one. The first thanks God who commanded us la'asok b'divrei Torah, to busy ourselves with the words of Torah. Not just to read, or to finish, but to be busy with it, the way you're busy with work. The next asks: make the words of Torah sweet in our mouths, and in the mouths of our children and their children. Sweet, the way honey is sweet. And the last is the one the Talmud calls the finest of blessings: who chose us and gave us the Torah. Then comes the part that makes the morning feel like a classroom. Right after the blessing, the prayer book gives a few lines to study, so the blessing has something to bless. In many prayer books, the first lines are the priestly blessing from the Book of Numbers, in the old Jewish translation: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee." Then a passage from the Mishnah, the list you heard yesterday. A verse, a law, a story: one from each layer of the tradition. The Talmud takes this blessing seriously. In tractate Nedarim, it even suggests that when learned people's children didn't become learned, it was because their parents hadn't blessed the Torah first. Study, in this telling, isn't only information. It's meant to be received as a gift, with thanks, before you open it.
screen: `TO BUSY OURSELVES WITH TORAH.` · `MAKE THE WORDS SWEET.` · `THEN A FEW LINES, RIGHT AWAY.` · `RECEIVED AS A GIFT, WITH THANKS.` · then, large: `LEARN SOMETHING FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say a blessing, then read one line. Settle, and breathe. Pick up something worth learning from: a page of scripture, a book you trust, even the line in today's lesson. If you pray, you can say the words of the priestly blessing first, or simply the Hebrew la'asok b'divrei Torah. If you don't, take one breath of thanks for being able to read at all. Then read one line, slowly, twice. Let it be the first thing you take in today, ahead of the news. The bell holds the time.
Learning before breakfast. The morning blessing over Torah, followed at once by a few lines of study.
Your line: learn something first. Tomorrow morning, before you open any app, read one line of something worth learning. Day five hundred forty-eight.

549.title: The binding in the morning
549.hook: many read the binding of Isaac each morning, asking for Abraham's devotion
549.howItsDone: Many Orthodox prayer books print the akedah (Genesis 22) near the start of the morning service with a request that follows it; some people say it privately each day, while other communities and prayer books leave it out.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the blessing over Torah, with study right after. Your line was learn something first. What was your first line this morning? Today, one of the hardest stories in the Torah, read at the start of the day. Day five hundred forty-nine.

Genesis, chapter twenty-two. God tells Abraham to take his son Isaac up a mountain and offer him there. Abraham rises early, saddles the donkey, splits the wood. Father and son walk together for three days. On the mountain, Abraham builds an altar, binds his son, and lifts the knife. And an angel calls out and stops him. It's a story people have argued over for thousands of years. Some of the most honest readers say it frightens them. And yet many Jews read this exact story every single morning, before breakfast.
screen: `GENESIS 22.` → `A FATHER, A SON, A KNIFE.` → `READ EVERY MORNING.`

segments.voice: In Hebrew it's called the akedah, the binding, from the word for tying Isaac's hands and feet. The old Jewish translation opens the chapter: "God did prove Abraham." A test. When God calls, Abraham answers, "Here am I," and at the end, when the angel calls, he answers the same way. And the angel says: "Lay not thy hand upon the lad." Isaac isn't harmed. Why read it daily? The custom spread in the later Middle Ages, and the Shulchan Aruch, the sixteenth-century code of Jewish law, calls it good to say each morning. After the passage, many prayer books add a request. It goes roughly like this: just as Abraham held back his compassion to do your will, so may your compassion hold back your anger from us. Notice the move. Abraham's devotion becomes something his children ask God to remember. The tradition calls this zechut avot, the merit of the ancestors: the idea that what the founders gave still counts for those who come after. Jews read this story many ways. Some see the height of faith: a person willing to give everything. Others stress the ending: the God of this story stops the knife, and many teachers have read it as a rejection of child sacrifice. Some live with the question and never settle it. Reading it every morning doesn't settle it either. It keeps the question, and the devotion, close.
screen: `AKEDAH: THE BINDING.` · `HERE AM I.` · `LAY NOT THY HAND UPON THE LAD.` · `ZECHUT AVOT: THE ANCESTORS' MERIT.` · then, large: `REMEMBER THE BINDING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: recall one devotion you admire. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone, in your family, your history, your neighborhood, who gave something costly for what they believed or loved. A grandparent who crossed an ocean. A parent who worked two jobs. A friend who kept a promise when it hurt. Picture one moment of that devotion clearly. Then ask, quietly: what of theirs am I still living on? If you pray, you can ask God to remember them. The bell holds the time.
The binding in the morning. The akedah, Genesis twenty-two, read daily by many Jews, asking God to remember Abraham's devotion.
screen: `THE BINDING IN THE MORNING — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: remember the binding. Today, tell someone about the person whose devotion you pictured, so it's remembered by one more person. Day five hundred forty-nine.

550.title: What are we?
550.hook: a humble prayer: what are we, what is our life, yet we are your people
550.howItsDone: In many prayer books, the passage beginning 'master of all worlds' and 'what are we' follows the morning blessings and leads into ashreinu, followed by the first line of the Shema, said early in the service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the binding of Isaac, read each morning. Your line was remember the binding. Whose devotion did you tell someone about? Today, the prayer that comes right after it. Day five hundred fifty.

Stand at the edge of the ocean at night, or under a sky far from city lights, and something happens to the size of your problems. They shrink. So do you. It's a strange feeling, humbling and freeing at once. Most of the time we work hard to feel big: important, busy, needed. The prayer book, a few minutes into the morning, does the opposite on purpose. Right after the story of Abraham, it asks a question you'd expect from someone staring at the stars. What are we?
screen: `UNDER A SKY FULL OF STARS.` → `YOUR PROBLEMS SHRINK. SO DO YOU.` → `WHAT ARE WE?`

segments.voice: The prayer begins: master of all worlds, we don't lay our pleas before you because of our righteousness, but because of your great mercy. Then it asks, in a string of short questions: what are we? What is our life? What is our kindness, our goodness, our strength? The opening questions are old. A version appears in the Talmud, tractate Yoma, among confessions said on Yom Kippur, and the morning prayer book borrowed them for every day. Then it piles it on. Before you, the mighty are as nothing, the famous as if they'd never been, the wise as if they knew nothing. It even quotes Ecclesiastes: compared with the beasts, people have no advantage, for all is vanity. If the prayer stopped there, it would be bleak. It doesn't. The very next word is but. But we are your people, children of your covenant. Children of Abraham, whom you loved. The seed of Isaac, who was bound on the altar. The community of Jacob. And then the prayer turns all the way around: therefore we are obligated to thank you. How fortunate we are, how good is our portion, how pleasant our lot. In Hebrew, ashreinu. That's the shape: small, then loved, then grateful. It doesn't ask you to feel important. It asks you to feel small, and held, at the same time. A psalm asks it too: what is man, that God is mindful of him? The prayer's answer is: not much, and dearly loved.
screen: `NOT FOR OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS.` · `WHAT ARE WE? WHAT IS OUR LIFE?` · `BUT WE ARE YOUR PEOPLE.` · `ASHREINU: HOW FORTUNATE WE ARE.` · then, large: `SMALL, YET LOVED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feel small and loved at once. Settle, and breathe. Picture the earth from far away: one blue dot, and you somewhere on it, too small to see. Let that be fine. Let it take the weight off. Then bring to mind one person who loves you, or loved you once. Feel how big you are to them. Hold both pictures together: the tiny dot, and the face that lights up when you walk in. If you pray, you can say ashreinu, how fortunate we are. The bell holds the time.
What are we? A morning prayer that admits how small people are, then turns: but we are your people, and how fortunate we are.
Your line: small, yet loved. Today, when you feel too important, or not important enough, remember the dot and the face. Day five hundred fifty.

551.title: Words instead of bulls (Hosea 14:3)
551.hook: since the Temple fell, reading about the offerings stands in for them
551.howItsDone: Orthodox prayer books print the passages on the daily offering, the incense and the places of the offerings early in the morning service, and many people read them daily; other movements' prayer books shorten, recast or omit them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prayer that asks what are we, and answers: your people. Your line was small, yet loved. When did you feel both? Today, a part of the morning many people skip past without knowing why it's there. Day five hundred fifty-one.

Open a traditional prayer book to the early morning pages and you'll find something surprising. Instructions for animal offerings. The daily lamb, morning and evening. The recipe for the Temple incense, ingredient by ingredient. Where in the Temple each offering was slaughtered. There hasn't been a Temple in Jerusalem since the Romans burned it in the year seventy. So why are these pages here, in a book people carry to work on the train? The answer starts with a prophet, and a strange phrase: the bulls of our lips.
screen: `OFFERINGS IN THE PRAYER BOOK.` → `NO TEMPLE SINCE THE YEAR 70.` → `THE BULLS OF OUR LIPS.`

segments.voice: The Hebrew word is korbanot, offerings, from a root that means to come near. An offering was a way of drawing close. When the Temple stood, priests offered a lamb every morning and every evening, the tamid, the constant offering. Then it was gone. How do you draw near without an altar? The rabbis found an answer in the prophet Hosea. In the old Jewish translation: "Take with you words, and return unto the LORD." And a few lines on: "so will we render for bullocks the offering of our lips." Words, standing where the bulls once stood. The Talmud, in tractate Taanit, tells a story. Abraham asks God: when my children have no Temple, how will they be forgiven? And God answers: I have already arranged for them the order of the offerings. Whenever they read it, I will count it as if they had brought them. So the prayer book prints the passages, and people read them. The Talmud also holds that the daily prayers themselves were set to match the times of the daily offerings, though it records another view too: that the patriarchs began them. Jewish communities treat these pages differently today. Orthodox prayer books keep them, and many add prayers for the Temple's rebuilding. Reform prayer books generally removed them. Conservative prayer books have often kept some readings while recasting the requests as remembrance. All of them share the core idea: words can carry what used to be carried on an altar.
screen: `KORBANOT: COMING NEAR.` · `TAKE WITH YOU WORDS.` · `READ IT, AND IT COUNTS.` · `COMMUNITIES KEEP IT DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `WORDS INSTEAD OF OFFERINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say words in place of an offering. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you would give, if giving were simple: an apology you owe, a thank you you never said, a promise you want to make. In the old world it might have been a lamb. Here it's words. Shape them slowly, until they're true. Then say them, quietly, out loud. If you pray, you can offer them to God. If not, offer them to the person they belong to, in your mind, and maybe later in person. The bell holds the time.
Korbanot. Offerings, from the root for coming near. Since the Temple fell, the morning reading of them stands in their place.
Your line: words instead of offerings. Today, say the words you shaped to the person they belong to, in a call, a note or face to face. Day five hundred fifty-one.

552.title: Kaddish for the teachers
552.hook: a Kaddish praying for teachers, their students and their students' students
552.howItsDone: Kaddish d'Rabbanan is said in a minyan after a passage of rabbinic study, including in the morning service after the readings on the offerings; mourners often lead it, and the congregation answers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, korbanot, the offerings read in place of the altar. Your line was words instead of offerings. Did you say the words to the person they belonged to? Today, the prayer that closes that section. Day five hundred fifty-two.

Think of the teacher who changed something for you. Maybe a fourth-grade teacher who read aloud with all the voices. A coach. A grandmother at a kitchen table. Now think of who taught them. And who taught that person. Somewhere back along that line is a stranger whose patience you're still living on, and you'll never know their name. Jewish prayer has a moment set aside for that whole invisible line. It comes right after a few minutes of study, and it's one of the forms of the Kaddish.
screen: `THE TEACHER WHO CHANGED SOMETHING.` → `AND WHO TAUGHT THEM?` → `AN INVISIBLE LINE.`

segments.voice: Most people know the Kaddish as the mourner's prayer. In fact it comes in several forms, and all of them share a core, in Aramaic, the everyday language of many Jews in the age of the Talmud: may God's great name be made great and holy in the world. The congregation answers: may God's great name be blessed forever. The Kaddish d'Rabbanan, the Kaddish of the rabbis, is said after a group has studied rabbinic teaching together. In the morning service it comes at the end of the readings you heard about yesterday. And it adds one paragraph that no other Kaddish has. It asks for blessing on Israel, and on the teachers, and on their students, and on all their students' students, and on everyone who studies Torah, here and in every place. It asks for peace, grace, kindness and compassion, long life, enough to live on, and help from heaven. Notice how far it reaches. Not just my teacher. The teachers, the students, the students of the students, spreading out across places and generations. Like every Kaddish, it's said only with a minyan, ten adults, and often mourners lead it. The Talmud, in tractate Sotah, says the world is held up by the response to the Kaddish said after study. Learning isn't treated as private. It ends with a prayer for everyone who carried it to you, and everyone you'll carry it to.
screen: `KADDISH: MAY THE NAME BE HALLOWED.` · `SAID AFTER STUDYING TOGETHER.` · `TEACHERS, STUDENTS, THEIR STUDENTS.` · `ONLY WITH A MINYAN.` · then, large: `PRAY FOR THE TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold a teacher in mind. Settle, and breathe. Bring back the face of one teacher who mattered to you, living or gone. Remember one thing they said or did that stayed. Then widen the picture: their teacher, behind them, and behind that one, a line going back further than you can see. Then look forward: the people you've taught, even a little, a child, a friend, a coworker. If you pray, you can ask God's peace for the whole line. If not, simply wish it to them. The bell holds the time.
Kaddish d'Rabbanan. The Kaddish of the rabbis, said after study, with a paragraph for teachers and their students' students.
Your line: pray for the teachers. Today, send a short thank you to one teacher, or tell someone else about them if you can't reach them anymore. Day five hundred fifty-two.

553.title: Warming up
553.hook: psalms before the main prayer, to prepare the heart
553.tomorrow: Blessed is the one who spoke
553.howItsDone: Pesukei d'Zimra is said each morning between the morning blessings and the Shema, opening with Baruch She'amar and closing with Yishtabach; on Shabbat and festivals more psalms are added, and many communities sing parts of it aloud.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kaddish of the rabbis, for teachers and their students' students. Your line was pray for the teachers. Which teacher did you thank? That closes the morning blessings. Today, a new part of the prayer book. Day five hundred fifty-three.

No singer walks onstage cold. Backstage there are scales, humming, lip trills, the odd noises that loosen a voice. Runners jog before they run. Even a hard conversation goes better if you've had a minute to breathe in the car first. The body and the heart both need a ramp. The Jewish morning service has one built in. Before the Shema, before the standing prayer at its center, there's a long stretch of psalms and songs whose job, more or less, is to warm you up.
screen: `NO SINGER WALKS ON COLD.` → `THE HEART NEEDS A RAMP.` → `A STRETCH OF SONGS FIRST.`

segments.voice: It's called Pesukei d'Zimra, verses of song. It opens with a blessing, Baruch She'amar, closes with another, Yishtabach, and between them come psalms and passages of praise. Where does the idea come from? The Mishnah, in tractate Berakhot, remembers that the early pious ones would wait an hour before praying, to direct their hearts. The Talmud adds a principle from Rabbi Simlai: a person should always first set out the praise of God, and only then ask for anything. He learns it from Moses, who begins his plea to God with praise before he asks to enter the land. And in tractate Shabbat, Rabbi Yose says: may my portion be among those who complete the praise every day. The Talmud explains he meant these verses of song, the psalms near the end of the Book of Psalms. So the order is deliberate. Thanks for waking, then a little study, then song, and only then the central prayers. Praise before asking. Warmth before words of need. Some teachers love a play on the word zimra. The same three Hebrew letters can mean to sing and to prune, as you prune a vine. So the verses of song can be heard as verses of pruning: cutting away the distractions so the prayer can grow. That's wordplay, not the word's history, but people find it true to the experience.
